headline: New-moon springs set up a sunset striper window from Kings Point to Matinecock
subhead: Bunker still stacked, tide stages lining up with dusk, and the first real PM bite since the June full moon is back on the table.
body_markdown:
We're coming off a stretch of typical mid-summer chop out here — small tides, slack current windows that dragged on too long, and bait that sat deep and unbothered through most of the daylight hours. Last week's tides were unremarkable, which in my book usually means unremarkable fishing, and that's about what I heard from the guys working Execution Rocks and the Stepping Stones reef — some marks on the bunker schools, not much commitment from the bass underneath them. Water in the back bays and coves has been running warm, and that heat has done exactly what warm water does in July: pushed bait and predators alike toward structure with current and depth, and away from the flats.

What's changing this week is the moon. We're building into new-moon springs, and that means bigger swings on the tide boards from Kings Point out through Hart Island. The number that matters to me is the way the PM flood is now lining up with sunset — that high-stand-at-dusk setup at Kings Point is the first real evening window we've had since the June full moon, and it's tightening in through the weekend with peak alignment landing July 11 through 13. When the flood stacks bait against structure right as the light goes low, the bass that have been sulking on bottom all day get up and hunt. That's not a guess, that's thirty years of watching this exact tide-and-light combination turn a dead evening into a good one at the Neck and around Stepping Stones.

So here's where I'd put my time. Bunker schools are still holding off Matinecock Point, same pattern we've seen since June, and there are keeper bass shadowing them in 15 to 25 feet on the drop toward the channel. Snag one on a weighted treble, no weight, and let it swim on a slow drift with the outgoing — you don't need a balloon out there, the current does the work. If you want more control, live-line a bunker under a small float and work it right along the edge where the school thins out, because that's where the bigger fish sit picking off stragglers instead of muscling into the pack. Execution Rocks is still doing what it always does on the outgoing — current wraps the rockpile and creates that seam on the north side, and bucktails in white or chartreuse, 1.5 to 2 ounce depending on how hard it's ripping, worked slow along bottom, have been picking up bass in the 26 to 34 inch range. Nothing epic, but honest fish, and enough of them that two or three rods working that seam on a good outgoing will put fish in the box.

Stepping Stones remains the spring-into-summer highway it's always been, and with this new PM window opening up, that's exactly where I'd want to be positioned an hour before the top of the flood through the first hour of the drop, right as the light fades. Troll bunker spoons or tube-and-worm along the light structure, or if you're a jig guy, work soft plastics — 5-inch paddle tails in bunker or white — on a slow retrieve through the rip line. This is a pattern I've fished for three decades: springs plus sunset plus that structure equals feeding fish. Doesn't mean every trip connects, but the conditions are about as aligned as they get this time of year.

Fluke have mostly abandoned the shallow bay water — it's just too warm in the coves and harbors right now, pushing into the upper 70s in spots like Manhasset and parts of Hempstead Harbor, and that's above where doormats want to sit. They've slid to the channel edges and the deeper cuts near Throgs Neck and the mouth of Little Neck Bay, where cooler water still holds along bottom. Four-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow through 25 to 35 feet on the last of the outgoing, have been the play. It's not a banner fluke week — I'd call it a working bite, a fish here and there rather than a limit trip — but the ones coming over the rail have had some size to them, a few pushing 5 pounds off the deeper edges near Execution Rocks.

Porgies are doing what porgies do — reliable, unglamorous, and exactly what you want if you're taking kids or just want dinner. Hart Island and the rock piles around Stepping Stones are stacked with them in 20 to 30 feet. Hi-lo rigs, small hooks, sandworm or clam, bottom fished on the anchor — you'll load the cooler without much drama.

Blackfish season's closed through the summer, so leave the crab pots home till fall reopens. And weakfish — I'll be straight with you, I haven't heard of a legitimate weakfish crossing a scale in this zone in weeks. The water's been plenty warm enough on paper, but warm water alone hasn't been the trigger people hoped for. I'm not chasing them right now, and I wouldn't plan a trip around it.

Looking ahead: if the wind stays reasonable through the weekend, I'd fish the Friday and Saturday evening flood at Stepping Stones and Kings Point hard — that's the best-aligned window we've had in a month. If the bass don't show on the surface, I've got bucktails ready to go deep along the rock edges at Execution Rocks as a fallback. Either way, bring the fluke rod for the ride home on the last of the outgoing — that bite's been steady enough to fill the gap.
